summary.text: Marble is a metamorphic rock made of carbonate minerals, most often calcite or dolomite, that have recrystallized under heat and pressure.
It forms from carbonate rocks such as limestone or dolomite, and its swirls and veins come from impurities like clay, sand or iron oxides in that original rock.
Its hardness, durability and polishable surface make it a building stone, and its even grain and light-scattering surface suit fine sculpture.

facts.label: Word origin
facts.value: Greek for crystalline rock, shining stone

items.prompt: A marble statue of a face looks soft and almost alive, with a waxy glow. What causes that look?

options.label: A coat of wax the sculptor applied
Light entering the stone and scattering out
Tiny mirror-like flakes on the surface
Water slowly seeping through the stone

items.explain: Light travels a little way into marble before being scattered back out, giving the waxy, lifelike look sculptors value.

items.prompt: A quarry yields perfectly white marble with no veins at all. What was its starting rock most likely like?

options.label: Mudstone rich in clay
Sandstone stained with iron
Granite full of crystals
Very pure limestone

items.explain: Pure white marble comes from metamorphism of very pure, silicate-poor limestone or dolomite.

items.prompt: Why do so many marbles show colored swirls and veins?

options.label: Impurities in the original rock
Cracks later filled by rainwater
Dye added during quarrying
Tree roots that grew through it

items.explain: Veins and swirls usually come from impurities like clay, sand or iron oxides in the original limestone, recrystallized during metamorphism.

items.prompt: Someone plans to clean a marble countertop with vinegar. Why is that a bad idea?

options.label: Its smell soaks into the stone
It leaves a sticky sugar film
Acids damage marble
It is too weak to remove dirt

items.explain: Acidic solutions like vinegar should be avoided on marble; acid rain likewise damages outdoor marble statues and gravestones.

items.prompt: A stone sold as Tennessee marble turns out, to geologists, to be a limestone. How can it still carry the name?

options.label: It was mislabeled by accident
The stone trade uses the word more loosely
All limestone becomes marble once polished
Geologists renamed it as a courtesy

items.explain: In geology marble means metamorphosed limestone, but in the stone trade the term covers other crystalline, polishable rocks too.

items.prompt: A geologist checks a piece of marble for the original layers and textures of its parent limestone. What will she typically find?

options.label: They are perfectly preserved
They are sharper than before
They have turned to gas pockets
They are altered or wiped out

items.explain: Recrystallization into an interlocking mosaic of carbonate crystals typically modifies or destroys the original sedimentary textures and structures.
